title: Rishabh Garg, Tesla Optimus — Challenges in High Performance Robotics Systems
talk_summary: A Tesla Optimus engineer walks through a toy robot control loop to show that many apparent 'policy' failures are actually software-system bugs: bus saturation, TX/RX thread desynchronization, logging stalls, and priority inversion. The core lesson is to instrument the wire (external bus capture, cycle-time plots) and separate real-time control from blocking work like logging.

takeaways.technique: External wire-tap instrumentation for agent runs
takeaways.what_they_do: They attach a cheap external transceiver to the CAN bus and run can-dump on a separate laptop to timestamp every message, then plot cycle times to distinguish policy faults from system faults.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we connect it to the canvas and we get data off the canvas... run utilities like can dump which will actually give you a timestamp data of what message was seen at what time
takeaways.numbers: 2ms target loop; observed 4ms gaps and near-zero gaps between adjacent messages

takeaways.technique: Move blocking I/O off the control loop
takeaways.what_they_do: Logging to disk froze the control loop for 30ms on a Raspberry Pi; they added a third CPU dedicated to logging so the real-time loop never blocks on disk.
takeaways.evidence_quote: your robot would stay frozen for 30 milliseconds as we saw on a Raspberry Pi with an SD card... we just add another CPU and now all our logging is handled by that third CPU
takeaways.numbers: 30ms freeze from a single disk-logging event

takeaways.what_they_do: They split TX, RX, and policy into separate threads and stagger them so RX for the next iteration overlaps policy compute, but warn that unsynchronized threads cause batched/duplicated sends and skipped inputs.

takeaways.technique: Avoid priority inversion in shared scheduler
takeaways.what_they_do: Boosting all process priorities starved the kernel that delivers the data, causing multi-second dropouts; fix was setting correct relative priorities across the pipeline.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we tend to just boost the priority of all our processes so high that we start just blocking the kernel almost
takeaways.numbers: dropouts of 'seconds almost at a time'

takeaways.technique: Bounded logging to avoid feedback blackout
takeaways.what_they_do: On microcontrollers, logging a dropped packet took long enough to drop the next packet, cascading into a full bus blackout; lesson is to rate-limit/decouple diagnostic logging.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you drop the next packet, you log again... you just keep logging and you see a complete blackout
